title: Local Excitation, Global Inhibition
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter works through a single model of spontaneous pattern formation: the Turing–Gierer–Meinhardt reaction-diffusion system for an activator molecule $a$ and an inhibitor molecule $i$. The question it answers is concrete — given a spatially uniform steady state that is stable against a *uniform* perturbation (more activator and inhibitor everywhere at once), what has to be true of the synthesis rates, decay rates and diffusion coefficients for that same steady state to be *unstable* against a spatial perturbation, so that a featureless field spontaneously wrinkles into a pattern? It assumes linear stability analysis of a $2\times 2$ system of ODEs (the trace–determinant test at a fixed point), the diffusion term in a reaction-diffusion PDE, and non-dimensionalization of a system of equations. ## The activator–inhibitor model Turing was the first to pose this kind of problem mathematically; Gierer and Meinhardt applied his formalism to a biological reaction network, which is why the model below is usually called the Turing–Gierer–Meinhardt theory. One of the first versions of it reads $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial a}{\partial t} &= r_a + k_a \frac{a^2}{i} - \gamma_a a + D_a \frac{\partial^2 a}{\partial x^2}, \\ \frac{\partial i}{\partial t} &= k_i a^2 - \gamma_i i + D_i \frac{\partial^2 i}{\partial x^2}. \end{aligned} $$ Read term by term. The activator $a$ is made at a constant, "leaky" rate $r_a$ — a leaky promoter, say — plus an autocatalytic term $k_a a^2/i$ that grows with $a$ and is suppressed by $i$. Both species decay by first-order kinetics, at rates $\gamma_a$ and $\gamma_i$, and both diffuse in one spatial dimension, with diffusion coefficients $D_a$ and $D_i$. The inhibitor is synthesized at a rate proportional to $a^2$: the activator drives its own antagonist. So the feedback loop is: activator promotes itself and its inhibitor; inhibitor suppresses the activator. Diffusion is what lets this loop, run at one point in space, affect its neighbours. Where does the $a^2/i$ term come from? Suppose the activator only acts as a dimer and the inhibitor only as a monomer, and that the activator's synthesis rate is proportional to the probability of having an activator dimer bound *and* no inhibitor monomer bound. Writing each as a Hill/saturation function with association constants $K_a$ and $K_i$, $$ Y = \frac{K_a a^2}{1 + K_a a^2}\left(1 - \frac{K_i i}{1+K_i i}\right) = \frac{K_a a^2}{1+K_a a^2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+K_i i} \;\approx\; \text{const} \times \frac{a^2}{i}, $$ where the last step is the approximation that holds when $a$ is small compared with $K_a^{-1}$ and $i$ is large compared with $K_i^{-1}$: the activator dimer is rarely fully bound so the first factor is linear in $a^2$, and the inhibitor is present enough that the second factor is well approximated by $1/(K_i i)$. Note that the inhibitor's own production, $k_i a^2$, is exactly a Hill function of $a$ with Hill coefficient $n_H = 2$ — the same dimerization assumption drives both halves of the loop. ## Reducing the parameter count Nine parameters appear in the model above ($r_a, k_a, k_i, \gamma_a, \gamma_i, D_a, D_i$, plus the two association constants folded into the approximation). Before asking about stability it pays to non-dimensionalize, both to simplify the algebra and to see how many of those nine actually matter. First rescale time by the activator's own decay rate, and space by the distance the activator diffuses in that time: $$ \tau \equiv \gamma_a t, \qquad s \equiv \frac{x}{\sqrt{D_a/\gamma_a}}. $$ Substituting turns the model into $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial a}{\partial \tau} &= \frac{r_a}{\gamma_a} + \frac{k_a}{\gamma_a}\frac{a^2}{i} - a + \frac{\partial^2 a}{\partial s^2}, \\ \frac{\partial i}{\partial \tau} &= \frac{k_i}{\gamma_a} a^2 - \frac{\gamma_i}{\gamma_a} i + \frac{D_i}{D_a}\frac{\partial^2 i}{\partial s^2}. \end{aligned} $$ There is still freedom left to rescale the concentrations themselves: set $A \equiv a/a_0$ and $I \equiv i/i_0$ for constants $a_0, i_0$ still to be chosen. Substituting and then choosing $$ a_0 = \frac{r_a}{\gamma_a}, \qquad i_0 = \frac{k_i a_0^2}{\gamma_i} = \frac{k_i r_a^2}{\gamma_i \gamma_a^2} $$ — i.e. picking $a_0$ so the constant-synthesis term becomes exactly $1$, and $i_0$ so the two terms that drive $i$ collapse to a single factor — leaves a system with only three parameters: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial A}{\partial \tau} &= 1 + R\frac{A^2}{I} - A + \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial s^2}, \\ \frac{\partial I}{\partial \tau} &= Q(A^2 - I) + P\frac{\partial^2 I}{\partial s^2}, \end{aligned} $$ where $$ P = \frac{D_i}{D_a}, \qquad Q = \frac{\gamma_i}{\gamma_a}, \qquad R = \frac{k_a \gamma_i}{r_a k_i}. $$ $P$ and $Q$ compare the inhibitor's diffusion coefficient and decay rate to the activator's; $R$ compares the strength of the autocatalytic term $k_a$ to the leaky, constant term $r_a$ — it is large when the activator's self-enhancement dominates its baseline synthesis. ## The spatially uniform steady state Set $\partial/\partial s = 0$ and look for the constant (spatially homogeneous) steady state. It is $$ \overline{A} = R+1, \qquad \overline{I} = (R+1)^2. $$ Is it stable against a uniform perturbation? Linearizing the reaction terms at this fixed point gives the stability (Jacobian) matrix $$ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2R\overline{A}}{\overline{I}} - 1 & -\dfrac{R\overline{A}^2}{\overline{I}^2} \\[4pt] 2\overline{A}Q & -Q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{R-1}{R+1} & -\dfrac{R}{(R+1)^2} \\[4pt] 2(R+1)Q & -Q \end{bmatrix}. $$ The standard test for a $2\times 2$ linear system applies: the fixed point is stable exactly when the trace is negative and the determinant is positive. Working the determinant out, $-Q(R-1)/(R+1) + 2RQ/(R+1) = Q$, which is positive automatically since $Q>0$ by definition — so that condition costs nothing. What has to be imposed is the trace condition, $$ \frac{R-1}{R+1} < Q. $$ So there is a unique constant solution, and it is stable against small spatially *uniform* disturbances whenever this inequality holds. The next question is whether it can still be unstable against a disturbance that varies in space — this is the condition that actually matters for pattern formation, since a real perturbation is never perfectly uniform. ## Turing instability: letting the perturbation vary in space Write the full solution as the steady state plus a perturbation, $A = \overline{A} + A'(s,\tau)$, $I = \overline{I} + I'(s,\tau)$, and linearize the full reaction-diffusion system around $(\overline A,\overline I)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial A'}{\partial \tau} &= \frac{R-1}{R+1}A' - \frac{R}{(1+R)^2}I' + \frac{\partial^2 A'}{\partial s^2}, \\ \frac{\partial I'}{\partial \tau} &= 2Q(1+R)A' - QI' + P\frac{\partial^2 I'}{\partial s^2}. \end{aligned} $$ Because the second derivative of a cosine is the cosine itself times a constant, a single spatial Fourier mode is an exact trial solution: try $$ A'(s,\tau) = \hat A(\tau)\cos(s/\ell), \qquad I'(s,\tau) = \hat I(\tau)\cos(s/\ell) $$ for a wavelength parameter $\ell$. Substituting turns the PDE pair into an ODE pair for the mode amplitudes, $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{d\hat A}{d\tau} &= \left(\frac{R-1}{R+1} - \frac{1}{\ell^2}\right)\hat A - \frac{R}{(1+R)^2}\hat I, \\ \frac{d\hat I}{d\tau} &= 2Q(1+R)\hat A - \left(Q + \frac{P}{\ell^2}\right)\hat I, \end{aligned} $$ which is exactly the same kind of $2\times 2$ linear system as before — diffusion has simply shifted the effective decay rates by $1/\ell^2$ and $P/\ell^2$. Apply the trace–determinant test again. The trace condition is guaranteed by the uniform-mode stability already imposed above, so it is the determinant condition that decides everything: $$ -\left(\frac{R-1}{R+1} - \frac{1}{\ell^2}\right)\left(Q+\frac{P}{\ell^2}\right) + \frac{2QR}{1+R} > 0. $$ Multiplying through by $\ell^2$ and collecting terms, this is equivalent to $$ \left(\frac{Q}{P}\right)\ell^4 + \left(\frac{Q}{P} - \frac{R-1}{R+1}\right)\ell^2 + 1 > 0. $$ If $$ \frac{Q}{P} > \frac{R-1}{R+1} $$ then this holds for *every* wavelength $\ell$ — no spatial mode can grow, and the uniform state is stable against all perturbations, not just uniform ones. Both this condition and the earlier trace condition are certainly satisfied if $P < 1$, i.e. if the activator diffuses faster than the inhibitor. Turning that around: spatial pattern formation is only possible if the *inhibitor* diffuses faster than the activator — short-range activation together with long-range inhibition. That phrase is the title of the model, and it is now a precise mathematical statement rather than a slogan. ## When does the uniform state actually go unstable? The reverse of the stability condition above is the condition for pattern formation. Writing $\alpha \equiv \ell^2$, instability requires $$ f(\alpha) \equiv \left(\frac{Q}{P}\right)\alpha^2 + \left(\frac{Q}{P} - \frac{R-1}{R+1}\right)\alpha + 1 < 0 $$ for some $\alpha$. Since $Q/P > 0$, $f$ is an upward-opening parabola in $\alpha$; for it to dip below zero it needs two real roots with at least one of them positive. The roots are $$ 2\alpha\frac{Q}{P} = \frac{R-1}{R+1} - \frac{Q}{P} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{R-1}{R+1}-\frac{Q}{P}\right)^2 - 4\frac{Q}{P}}, $$ which are real precisely when $$ \left(\frac{R-1}{R+1} - \frac{Q}{P}\right)^2 > 4\frac{Q}{P}. $$ Given the stability condition from the previous section, this discriminant condition forces both roots to be positive, so the full instability condition collapses to $$ \frac{R-1}{R+1} > 2\sqrt{\frac{Q}{P}} + \frac{Q}{P}. $$ This defines a critical value of $R$: instability sets in once $R$ exceeds $$ R_c = \frac{1 + \left(2\sqrt{Q/P} + Q/P\right)}{1 - \left(2\sqrt{Q/P} + Q/P\right)}. $$ **The strong-autocatalysis limit.** When the autocatalytic term dominates the leaky one, $R \gg 1$, the left side above tends to $1$ and the instability condition simplifies to $$ \frac{Q}{P} + 2\sqrt{\frac{Q}{P}} < 1, $$ which (solving the resulting quadratic in $\sqrt{Q/P}$) means $$ \sqrt{\frac{Q}{P}} = \left(\frac{D_a/\gamma_a}{D_i/\gamma_i}\right)^{1/2} < 0.4. $$ The quantity $(D_a/\gamma_a)^{1/2}$ has units of length: it is the typical distance an activator molecule diffuses before it decays, the *activator range*. The same combination for the inhibitor is the *inhibitor range*. So the condition for a strongly autocatalytic activator-inhibitor system to break spontaneously into a spatial pattern is that the inhibitor range be roughly $1/0.4 \approx 2.5$ times larger than the activator range — the "long-range inhibition, short-range activation" condition made quantitative. ## Sources - Lecture outline "VIII Local excitation, global inhibition model" (MIT OCW 8.591J, 2004, lecture 15 outline), all four sections: the model and its saturation function (`01-viii-local-excitation-global-inhibition-model.md`); non-dimensionalization and the uniform steady state (`02-dimensionless-variables.md`); the spatial-perturbation analysis and the short-range-activation/long-range-inhibition condition (`03-spatially-inhomogeneous-solutions.md`); the instability threshold, $R_c$, and the strong-autocatalysis limit (`04-conditions-for-inhomogeneous-instability.md`). - No transcript, written notes or exercise set were supplied for this lecture — the outline above is the entire source. That outline was itself reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no text layer (`sources/ocw-8591j/2004/lecture-outlines/15-outline.pdf`), and its own header flags every equation in it as unverified against the original slide; the equations above are reproduced as given wherever the algebra checks out. - One inconsistency was found and corrected: the outline's equations for the quartic in $\ell$ (`VIII.18`), the parabola $f(\alpha)$ (`VIII.20`), its roots (`VIII.21`) and its discriminant (`VIII.22`) all carry $(R+1)/(R-1)$, but expanding the determinant condition two equations earlier (`VIII.17`) gives $(R-1)/(R+1)$ — and the outline's own next steps (`VIII.19` and the final instability condition `VIII.23`) use $(R-1)/(R+1)$ too. This chapter uses $(R-1)/(R+1)$ throughout, matching the surrounding equations and independently verified by expanding `VIII.17` directly.
